newsitem.title: USA: Dollar soars as wariness of central banks diminishes.
newsitem.headline: Dollar soars as wariness of central banks diminishes.

text.p: The dollar advanced to a three-year high against the German mark and extended its rally against the Japanese yen to a new 4-1/2-year peak amid easing fears that central banks would try to end its climb.
The U.S. economy's relative strength and the upward trajectory of interest rates also continued to bolster the dollar.

The dollar reached its highest level since August 1992 against the yen in New York trading, continuing the climb that came after Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin denied speculation he had discussed curbing the dollar's rise with senior Japanese officials in Tokyo last week.
The dollar also topped its March high against the mark. Investors expecting further gains in the dollar bought agressively, catapulting it to 1.7270 marks, its highest level since February 1994.

"It's nothing new ... just a general belief that central banks are not going to be concerned about a move higher, so in the market's mind they've gotten the green light to take it higher," said Richard Vullo, a vice president at Bayerische Hypothenken und Weschelsbank.
The dollar ended at 126.80 yen, up from 126.30 Tuesday, and at 1.7255 marks, up from 1.7155 marks.

Wariness of possible central bank action has slowed the dollar's rise since February when finance officials from the Group of Seven industrial nations said the dollar's rally from record lows in 1995 had corrected major misalignments in exchange rates.
Japanese officials in particular have seemed to want to stem the dollar's rise, worried that the weak yen might do additional damage to their fragile financial markets.

In early overseas trading, the dollar shrugged off remarks by Eisuke Sakakibara, the director-general of the Japanese Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, who said Japanese intervention in the currency markets was possible if exchange rates get substantially out of line with relative economic conditions in Japan and the United States.

But after the quarter-point interest rate increase by the Federal Reserve on March 25, investors comparing the stumbling economies of Japan and Europe to robust U.S. growth view conditions as highly favourable for the dollar.

"There is very little advantage to hold marks. I mean it's a very expensive proposition right now, based on interest rates and the prospects for just general growth in Europe vs. America," said Diego Giurleo, a vice president at Royal Bank of Canada in New York.
"If you look at the yen, there is the other issue, which is the weakness of the (Japanese) financial system, which more or less precludes any tightening in monetary policy there," Giurleo added.
Elsewhere, the dollar rose to 1.4788 Swiss francs from 1.4748 Swiss and to Canadian $1.3895 from C$1.3885. Britain's pound fell to $1.6200 from $1.6260.
